newsitem.title: FRANCE: French capital markets closing report.
newsitem.headline: French capital markets closing report.

text.p: French bond futures finished MATIF trading lower on Wednesday amid market talk of private opinion polls showing the left well placed ahead of Sunday's election runoff and weakness in the German bond market.
The franc too slipped to 3.3828 before pulling back.

Analysts said the stock market had suffered more than bonds as share investors got to grips with the possibility of a left win in the wake of Sunday's first round vote but predicted more, if less marked, pressure on debt in coming days.
The next two days could prove a little nail-biting, traders said, noting that they believed buyer support was likely to lift the market after the weekend, even if the left came to power.
Analysts put Wednesday's weakness in bond futures down to a mix of poll talk and the knock-on effect of market rumours that Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer had or planned to resign.
A Bundesbank spokeswoman told Reuters that "this rumour has absolutely no basis in fact".

The June 10-year bond future had opened stronger but lost ground amid poll and the German Tietmeyer talk to finish at 128.16 on MATIF, with the low-point of the day, 128.06, still higher than the lows of the past two days.
It stood at 128.44 on GLOBEX at 1540 GMT, well above the low hit on Monday in the wake of the left's surprise first-round vote lead on Sunday night.

Analysts said the market was likely to remain fragile as it finetuned its view on Socialist prospects for taking power but said the market already took a relatively sanguine view of the impact a win for the left would have on European monetary union.
Economist Philippe Brossard at ABN Amro said: "The odds have shifted this morning in the markets". Until today it had thought there was a 50 percent chance the right would win, he said.
He and other analysts noted that the Socialist party was not against EMU and was even likely to back off with time on the conditions it was attaching to support for a single currency.

Smith Barney economist Steven Englander said he believed that market worries on Wednesday probably had more to do with the talk of a Tietmeyer resignation and highlighted that the French stock market reaction to the left was more due to the "non-EMU part" of the Socialist manifesto.
PIBOR and the franc suffered more than bond futures in the face of the market turbulence with the currency slipping to a low of 3.3828 before regaining a little strength.
Foreign exchange traders said there was talk that the Bank of France had been intervening through mark-selling to support the franc at a level of 3.3775.

The central bank said, as is the tradition, that it had no comment, and traders contacted by Reuters said they had not directly seen intervention but cited heavy mark selling at around 3.3775 or 3.3780.
